name: Oshiroi white face powder

card.summary: A traditional Japanese white face powder used by geisha, maiko and kabuki actors to create a pale, even, porcelain-like complexion.
card.note: Historic versions contained white lead, banned in Japan in 1934; modern versions use non-lead ingredients.

quick.overview:
Oshiroi (white powder) is a Japanese foundation that gives the face and neck an opaque white finish. Geisha and maiko wear it for a porcelain look, and kabuki actors apply it thickly so the face reads from the back of the theatre.

It is also a base for colour work such as red lines at the eyes and the nape of the neck. Older oshiroi contained white lead; today's versions use rice powder, zinc oxide, kaolin and talc, with mixes that vary by maker.
quick.how: Traditional application mixes the powder with water to form a paste that is painted on in layers over a wax-based primer, with a gap left at the nape. Some modern wearers dust it over foundation or use it as a loose or pressed touch-up powder.
quick.risks: Lead-based oshiroi could cause lead poisoning in wearers over time; Japan prohibited white lead in makeup in 1934, according to Wikipedia (the date is flagged there as needing a citation). Modern products avoid lead. Heavy opaque makeup can irritate sensitive skin.

lead: Oshiroi is a traditional Japanese white powder foundation used by kabuki actors, geisha and maiko. Applied to the face and neck, it produces a bright, even, mask-like complexion that also serves as the base for other makeup details.[1][2]

Grokipedia describes it as introduced to Japan from China during the Asuka-Nara period and associated with nobility in the Heian period, when pale skin signalled a sheltered, high-status life. Its use widened in the Edo period among geisha and kabuki performers.[2]

Historic formulations used white lead, which could cause lead poisoning; non-lead rice-based versions were developed in the early twentieth century and lead was banned from makeup in Japan in 1934.[1][2]

chain: Apply opaque white powder over a primer
Pale, porcelain-like face with clean base for other makeup
angle.text: Oshiroi gives immediate, opaque coverage that lightens and evens the face and neck. Geisha use it as the canvas for lip and eye colour, and some modern wearers use it for touch-ups over foundation.

infobox: Introduced from China (Asuka-Nara period, per Grokipedia)
Rice powder, zinc oxide, kaolin, talc

paras: Oshiroi is mixed with water and applied over wax primers: ishineri on the eyebrows and bintsuke on the face, neck and sometimes the upper back, and is finished with rice powder.[1] Geisha and maiko leave two triangular bare stripes on the nape (eri-ashi), or three for formal occasions (sanbon-ashi).[1]
Kabuki actors apply it thickly so the face is bright from the back of the audience. Because it is opaque, an actor can paint over earlier makeup during a quick costume change.[1]

Grokipedia gives the origin as Chinese cosmetics imported during the Asuka-Nara period (538-794 CE), with the Heian period (794-1185) linking pale skin to nobility and widespread production emerging in Sakai by the Keicho era (1596-1615). It reports Shiseido's non-lead Hana Oshiroi in 1906 and Kanebo's stage version in 1954.[2] These details come from an AI-generated source and may differ from other accounts.
In Japanese aesthetics, pale skin has been associated with purity, nobility and freedom from outdoor work, captured in the proverb that white skin hides seven flaws.[2]
Lead-based oshiroi could eventually cause lead poisoning in wearers, with symptoms that include abdominal pain and neurological effects.[1][2] Modern formulations avoid lead.[1]

timeline.event: Widespread oshiroi production emerges in Sakai during the Keicho era, per Grokipedia.[2]
Shiseido introduces non-lead Hana Oshiroi, per Grokipedia.[2]
Japan outlaws white lead in makeup.[1]
Kanebo develops a non-lead oshiroi for kabuki, per Grokipedia.[2]
